sense: from a gun, or an arrow

terms.grammar: phrase: ictus, ictūs m. with the genitive of sclopētum
terms.comment: Classical ictus is a blow or stroke, and also the hit of a missile shot from an engine (ictū scorpiōnis, Caes. B.G. 7.25); with sclopētī it is the Renaissance phrase for a gunshot. A cannon shot is ictus tormentī (M-O s.v. gunfire).
Traupman’s verb. M-O gives sclopētum displōdere, to fire a gun, and plumbeā glande ferīre, to shoot someone (M-O s.v. gunshot).

terms.grammar: phrase: tēlum, tēlī n. with conjiciō, conjicere, conjēcī, conjectum
evidence: Caes. B.G. 1.26: tēla in nostrōs (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The classical way to say shooting, of bows, slings and spears: sagittās conjicere, to shoot arrows.

phrases.latin: nōn caecīs ictibus procul ex imprōvīsō vulnerābantur
phrases.english: they were not wounded by blind shots from afar, without warning

sources: Lewis & Short: ictus · Lewis & Short: conicio
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 324.
Morgan–Owens: Adumbratio, s.v. gunshot, gunfire.
